newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian premier to hold first talks with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Albanian premier to hold first talks with rebels.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino was expected to travel to the south of the country on Wednesday to talk to rebels who have seized control of the area and are demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha.

It would be Fino's first visit to the rebel-held south since he was appointed last week to head an all-party interim government charged with restoring order in the troubled Balkan country and organising new elections by June.
Fino is expected to travel to Gjirokaster, a stronghold of rebels who rose up against Berisha over failed savings schemes that bankrupted thousands and are demanding he quit by March 20.
The 34-year-old premier, a member of the ex-communist Socialist party that has been the main opposition for five years, is a native of Gjirokaster.
Local rebel leader Agim Ghozita, a former army general, told Reuters on Tuesday that if Berisha did not go they would elect their own presidential council to challenge him directly.

Ghozita said he was willing to work with the new government only if he stopped all cooperation with Berisha, accused by the rebels of failing to stop the shady schemes or warn the public of the risks.
However Ghozita stressed that the rebels wanted a political and not a military solution to the crisis which has rocked Albania for three weeks.

In Tirana parliamentary speaker Pjeter Arbnori described the rebels' ultimatum as an attempt to destabilise the country and called for all political parties to observe an agreement on national reconciliation signed with Berisha last week.
Berisha has pledged to step down if his Democratic Party which has ruled for five years loses the elections, but this has failed to satisfy the rebels.
The situation in Gjirokaster was reported to be volatile after gunmen raided the city's main bank on early on Tuesday and seized all the money in the vaults, which serve several surrounding towns.

In Tirana, the restoration of normal life after the armed anarchy that followed the looting of army barracks last week continued as the government announced the airport, closed last week, would reopen on Thursday.
However the situation on Albania's Adriatic coast continued to be chaotic as hundreds of people tried to flee to Italy by boat.
The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said over 2,500 people fled to Italy on Tuesday, more than on any single day to date, adding to nearly 10,000 already in Italy and Greece.

In Durres, Albania's main port 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana, nearly 100 people took a derelict freighter out of the harbour, using makeshift paddles, sails fashioned from garbage bags and the current.
The ship ran aground south of Durres and the passengers were brought back to shore by motorised rubber dinghies.
The chaos prompted marine insurance writers in London effectively to declare the area a war zone liable to increased premiums.
Concern was mounting in Italy that it could be facing a tide of illegal immigration and crime rather than a genuine refugee crisis.
Italy's chief anti-Mafia prosecutor, Pier Luigi Vigna, said he feared the exodus might include criminals released by the government during the armed anarchy that swept Albania.
